prompt.context: A fast food chain recently bought a bovine meat-processing outlet to supply it with fresh hamburgers and other meats. The shop process is: cows enter from one end of the shop, meat gets processed in the middle, and then the meat gets packaged and delivered at the other end.
prompt.question: The manager of the butcher shop could not decide whether to have the cows walk or run into the meat processing room. Can you help him?

clarifying_info.q: How many hamburgers can be made from each cow?
How many hours per day is the shop open?
clarifying_info.a: 10 hours per day, 5 days a week.

clarifying_info.q: How many cows can be processed per hour if they walk?
How many cows can be processed per hour if they run?
How many outlets does the fast food chain have?
clarifying_info.a: 10 outlets, and the meat-processing factory serves all 10.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population in each outlet's vicinity?
clarifying_info.a: Each outlet serves a vicinity of about 30,000 people.

clarifying_info.q: How many competitors are there in each vicinity?
clarifying_info.a: About 3 other competitors in each vicinity.

framework: Understand shop capacity: compare hamburgers produced per day under walk vs. run scenarios
Analyze cost implications: calculate total cost and cost per burger under each scenario
Estimate market size and demand: size the total addressable customer base and weekly burger demand
Match supply with demand: determine which capacity option is needed to meet (but not over-serve) actual demand

questions.prompt: Calculate the number of hamburgers the shop can produce per day if cows walk vs. run.
questions.guidance: Walk: 10 cows/hour × 10 hours/day × 20 burgers/cow = 2,000 burgers/day. Run: 25 cows/hour × 10 hours/day × 20 burgers/cow = 5,000 burgers/day.

steps: Weekly (5 days): Walk = 10,000 burgers/week; Run = 25,000 burgers/week

questions.prompt: Calculate and compare the cost per burger under the walk vs. run scenarios.
questions.guidance: Use the provided cost breakdown. Labor scales proportionally; overhead increases but not proportionally due to sunk costs. Walk: $6,000 total / 10,000 burgers = $0.60/burger. Run: $12,500 / 25,000 = $0.50/burger. Running is $0.10 cheaper per burger.

math.setup: Cost per burger = Total weekly cost / Burgers per week
steps: Difference: $0.60 - $0.50 = $0.10 savings per burger under run scenario

questions.prompt: Estimate the total weekly burger demand across all 10 outlets.
questions.guidance: Work through the funnel: total population → market share → demographic fit → frequency filter → visit frequency → burger order rate.

math.setup: Funnel: total population × market share × demographic % × regulars % × visits/week × burger order rate
steps: 10 outlets × 30,000 people each = 300,000 total population in all vicinities
Market share: 1 competitor out of 4 (25%) → 300,000 × 25% = 75,000 potential customers
Healthy-food trend filter (parents allow): 30,000 × 1/3 ≈ 10,000 regular customers
math.answer: Approximately 10,000 burgers per week across all 10 outlets

questions.prompt: Match supply with demand and determine whether walk or run is the right choice.
questions.guidance: Demand is 10,000 burgers/week. Walk scenario produces exactly 10,000 burgers/week — perfectly meeting demand. Run produces 25,000 burgers/week — 2.5× more than needed. Even though running lowers unit cost, there is no demand to support the extra supply. Walking meets demand and keeps meat fresh (lower inventory/waste risk).

math.setup: Compare weekly supply vs. weekly demand
steps: Run supply: 25,000 burgers/week >> Demand: 10,000 burgers/week (excess 15,000 burgers)
math.answer: Walk exactly meets demand; run produces 15,000 surplus burgers with no buyers

recommendation: Have the cows walk into the meat processing room.
Walking produces exactly 10,000 burgers per week, which matches estimated weekly demand across all 10 outlets.

Although running reduces cost per burger by $0.10 (from $0.60 to $0.50), producing 25,000 burgers/week against demand of only 10,000 creates 15,000 unsold burgers — generating waste and higher total costs with no incremental revenue.
risks: Demand could grow (new outlets, marketing success) — if so, re-evaluate the run scenario.
The 25% market share and demographic assumptions are estimates; actual demand could differ.
Overhead and labor cost figures assumed — actual cost structures may vary.
next_steps: Monitor actual burger demand weekly across all 10 outlets to validate the 10,000/week estimate.
Reassess the walk-vs-run decision if demand consistently approaches 10,000 burgers/week, since running would then become cost-advantageous.
Explore whether the 25% market share can be improved before scaling up production capacity.
